full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, C. J.—This appeal by the Commissioner of Income Tax, Dacca arises out of an application for a direction upon the Joint Official Liquidators, Dacca Electricity Development Co. Ltd. (In liquidation) to ray a sum of Rs. 15, 05,970/- to the Income Tax Department so as to credit the said amount as income tax and additional Income Tax due to the Government. 

 2. Facts of the case are practically not disputed. Case of the parties has been elaborately stated in the judgment under appeal. The facts which are relevant for consideration of the question raised in the appeal are like this; Dacca Electricity Development Company Ltd. was an assessee under the Income Tax Act. When making assessment for the year 1958-59 the Income Tax Officer took into account the price of the machinery, plants, building etc. purchased by the Government as empowered under the Electricity Act 1910; as en 31st May, 1957. The Government elected to purchase the undertaking with effect from 31st May, 1957 according to the terms of clause (c) of section 5 of the Electricity Act, 1910, as amended by the Electricity (East Pakistan Amendment) Ordinance, 1957, and also directed the Company to make over the possession of the undertaking to the Government on and from 31st May, 1957 according to the terms of clause (d) of section 5 of the Act. Licence of the Company was also revoked. The price offered by the Government was R.s. 70,00,844/- for the entire business including the machinery and plants. The company ceased to have any business on and from 31st May, 1957. Thereafter, the company was wound up on 23rd January, 1959 and Joint Official Liquidators were appointed by the High Court. The company did not accept the price offered by the Government and referred the matter to arbitration. The Arbitrator gave an award of Rs. 89,76,940/-. on 28th September, 1961; and against this award the Government preferred an appeal which was dismissed by the High Court on 27th April, 1965. Prayer for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 30th November 1965. Assessment was made for the assessment year 1958-59 based on the profit made by the Company by the sale of its plants and machineries which was calculated on the difference between the sale price and the written down book value. This arrangement was set aside by the Appellate Tribunal by its order dated 8th July, 1965. Income Tax Officer was directed to make fresh assessment in accordance with law. Fresh assessment made under section 23(3) read with section 33 of the Income Tax Act was also set aside by the Tribunal on the ground that the sale of the assets did not take place within the accounting year 1957-58 as the price had not yet been fixed and as such the amount was not taxable in the assessment year 1958-59. Thereafter on the basis of the award treating the income accrued in the year 1961 was assessed for accounting year 1961-62 and assessment year 1962-63 under sections 23(3)/34 of the Income Tax Act was completed on 10th October 1967 resulting in a total demand of Rs. 11,98,326/- Rs. 11,98,326/- was determined as the income tax demand on account of the above noted sale. The Commissioner of Income Tax filed an application on 24th June 1968 before the Company Judge of the Dacca High Court for giving direction upon the Joint Official Liquidators for raking adequate provision for payment of the outstanding demand of Rs. 11,98,326/- in respect of income tax and super tax for the assessment year 1962-63, from the funds of the Company in liquidation. Official Liquidators resisted the application who had earlier rejected the claim of the Commissioner, on two grounds, namely (i) claim before the Official Liquidators was barred by limitation as it had been filed after expiry of the date fixed for receiving the claims against the company; (ii) the assessment itself was bad as the assessment was made on the sale price of the assets acquired by the Government rant, although there was no sale of the assets; and (iii) the Company ceased to be an assesse and (iv) section 10(2) (vii) of the Income Tax Act has no application to the case. 

 3. The learned Company Judge on consideration of the materials placed before him took view that provisions of section 10(2) (vii) of the Income Tax Act as amended by the Finance Act of 1962 is not attracted: to the case, because, firstly the price offered by the Government was not for sale, but it was the price for acquisition of machinery, building etc. of the company and secondly the Company ceased to be a company and it also ceased to be an assessee. The learned Judge held that the order of assessment was bad in law. Accordingly the application filed by the Commissioner was dismissed. 

 6. The learned Advocate appearing for the Creditor, however, contended that in view of the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of M/s. Chittagong Engineering & Electric Supply Co. Ltd. Vs. Income Tax officer and others, 22 D.L.R. (S.C.) 443, assessment in respect of the price of the assets of the company compulsorily acquired by the Government, could not be assessed till it was finally determined. Quantum of price got the finality only when leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused, on 30th November, 1965. Before the price was finalised, it could not be made subject matter of the assessment. The learned Advocate also argued that the company having ceased to be an assessee because of the liquidation order; and the company having ceased to be a company on account of acquisition of all the assets the company having ceased to have any business, and consequently the company, having ceased to be an asses see there could not be any action for making assessment of income-tax for the assessment year 1962-63. The learned Advocate further argued that, in any view of the matter, section 10(2)(vii) of the Income Tax Act having no retrospective application to the price awarded by the Arbitrator in September, 1961, the order of assessment is bad in law, and as such, the claim of the appellant, was rightly rejected. 

 7. The learned Advocate appearing for the appellant made some submissions with reference to section 10(2)(vii) read with section 3 of the Income Tax Act, that in spite of the fact that the assets of the company were taken up by the Government by way of compulsory acquisition under the Electricity Act of 1910 and the company ceased to have any business, the price on account of the assets acquired by the Government could be made the subject matter of the assessment in view of the amended section 10(2) (vii) of the Income Tax Act, which is retrospective. This agreement of the learned Advocate also does not improve the appellant's case any further. We have already taken the view that until finality of the price was reached, the transaction could not be made I he subject matter of assessment of income-tax in this case with regard to the price of the assets it was finally decided when leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused, in November, 1965. It is true that the Arbitrator gave his award with regard to the price of the assets taken up by the Government in September, 1961, but the Government did not accept it and preferred appeal before the High Court and after dismissal of the appeal petition for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was filed but leave was refused. On the refusal to grant leave, the price of the assets reached the finality. It has been noted above that the previous assessment for the price of the self same assets for the year 1958-59 had been set aside by the Appellate Tribunal en 8th July, 1965, and fresh assessment was directed. Fresh assessment as per direction of the Appellate Tribunal was made treating the income accrued in the accounting years 1961-62 and assessment year 1962-63, Besides, the price of the assets in spite of the amendment of section 10(2)(vii) of the Income Tax Act providing that profits or gains even in respect of building, machinery or plants which have been compulsorily acquired and even after cessation of the business, could not be legally computed in the assessment of income tax for the accounting year 1961-62, and as such, the assessment order is bad in law. Reference to section 3 also does not improve the case. 

 8. Section 10(2)(vii) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 was amended by the Finance Act (Act 1 of 1962) with effect from 30th June, 1962, There is nothing in the amended section to show that it has been given retrospective application. For the purpose of assessment of income-tax on the price of the assets of the Company, even reference to section 3 of the Income-Tax Act does not enable the Income-Tax Officer to make the assessment. In this case, as noted above, finality of the price reached only when the petition for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused in 1965. Another significant position is that the Company in view of compulsory acquisition of all its assets by the Government and revocation of its licence by the Government ceased to be a company; and that the company having ceased to be a company and consequently it having no business, it also ceased to be an assessee. Finality of the price reached at a time when the company ceased to be an assessee. In any view of the matter the order of assessment was not valid, and the same has been rightly held so by the learned Judge.
